utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. As you can see, only two judges are present. Judge Nyambe can't be with us today and in the next week, so the Chamber decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, only with two judges these five hearing days. Yesterday, I mentioned the urgent motion of the Prosecution for leave to file an amended Rule 65 ter summary for Witness Erin Gallagher and for addition of one document to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. This is a confidential motion and I would like to ask the Defence if they are in a position to express their position to this motion. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are no objections to raise on our part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, the motion is granted. The amended Rule 65 ter summary and the addition of one document is permitted. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the only question that remains at issue since yesterday is P1224. That exhibit, it has been MFI'd, and the Defence asked for the exhibit to be admitted, but if I remember well, you raised the issue of whether that document should be assigned a P number or a D number. Therefore, we would just like to reiterate our motion for that document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are some documents remaining to be discussed, and we will come back to that later. Thank you for your intervention, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the solemn declaration to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace to everyone in this house and may God speed us on our way to a successful conclusion of today's session. May God bless you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. The last thing we talked about yesterday is you coming under attack by anti-aircraft guns and machine-guns when you were in Srebrenica. My question: Was there a single attack that you came under or did that continue throughout your clashes with the Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that the first time an attack occurred was on the 10th, after the unit changed its direction of engagement. That was just past the village of Slapovic. It was perhaps an hour before the entry into Srebrenica that the firing came from a variety of firing points and positions, and my unit came under attack as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell us whether at the time you were in direct combat contact with the Muslim forces or did you simply come under fire without knowing who was firing at you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my units are concerned, I wasn't really there in direct contact with the soldiers who were seizing territory and directly engaged in the fighting. I was observing all of this from certain points that had a clear view of the whole combat arena. Nevertheless, based on the reports that I was receiving and the communication I had with those officers who were in charge, especially the reconnaissance officers, it was definitely this unit that came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you told us that the first time you came under attack was on the 10th, at least as far as you were able to specify, could you please tell us this: Did you know that there were armoured units and UNPROFOR weapons also firing at you in keeping with an order that they had been given? Thank you. If you're not clear about the nature of this question, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do believe I've understood the question. It wasn't the UNPROFOR units firing at us. Not this attack. My unit and I met them directly, the UNPROFOR people. They crossed over to our side, if I can put it like that, in the Slapovici sector, and that was my area of operation. I don't know about anybody else, but as far as my unit was concerned, we did not come under attack by the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When he testified here, the deputy battalion commander of UNPROFOR Nastrani [phoen] or, rather, at page 3454, lines 23 through 25, the date was the 1st of July, said as follows, and I will quote this for you. We don't have the transcript in the Serbian language in front of us: "Ever since the green order was issued, we were engaging the VRS. The VRS was our target. And this applied the other way around as well." So he's saying this and he's talking about this order, and then he goes on to say this in 3473, lines 5 through 6. I asked him, When was the green order issued? and he said: "That had to be on the 9th of July and continued to apply throughout until the 11th, when the events in Srebrenica were over." Bearing this in mind, is there a possibility that there were some UNPROFOR weapons that were firing at you, in keeping with this order that came from their superiors? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as precise as I can. As far as I remember, from an earlier statement, I said myself that they had a crew there with an officer in charge, and an APC. They drove down to the Slapovici sector, but it wasn't before the 10th. We had reached Slapovici, the village itself, on the 9th. The morning of the 10th we actually entered the village. We went around the village and realised there were no people left there. As we were walking around, they came down from somewhere around Zivkovo Brdo and Vogan. There is a path that crosses the saddle between the two hills and they went down as far as the small bridge there. There is a creek there in Slapovici and a small bridge that crosses it. They were scared, they got out of the vehicle, raised their hands and surrendered, placed themselves under our control. Or that was the impression that I had at the time. They had probably been scared by rumours about Serbian soldiers killing people there. One of them in fact was so scared that he wet his pants when he set eyes on me and the soldiers who were with me. They left with me. I persuaded them that there was no reason to fear. One of the men who were with me was able to use the English language to some extent to communicate. They went with me as far as the command post. They had lunch there. They each had a beer. I informed the corps command that I had three or four men with me there, the crew that I told you about, and an officer who was with them. I'm talking about the UNPROFOR APC and an UNPROFOR crew. Someone from the command took over, I don't remember who it was that came for them. He took them away and the APC was driven by their own driver in the presence of another soldier who was from the corps command. Was it the corps staff? I can't remember anymore. That was the last I saw of them. But I can't say whether it was them firing at me. It was quite obvious they were scared. Maybe they were not willing to open fire when they saw us. We just met there and we found our own way to communicate and settle the situation as normal human beings, and then we parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. When did this event occur and where did these people go? Did they go back to the Muslim side or elsewhere? Just for the record, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were with me at the command post, therefore I informed the corps command and handed them over to the corps command. Handed them over. All right, I informed the corps command and then someone from the corps command came over and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the record, we state that the UNPROFOR men went away with representatives of the Drina Corps command after surrendering to Mr. Trivic. Mr. Trivic, could you please go to your own logbook now, page 5. That's how you marked it. That's 782, the copy that's been distributed to us. Could we please have ERN number 0648-6782 shown on our screens. This is Exhibit P1444. Thank you. We are waiting for it to come up. This is page 5 of your logbook. You record some bullet points there. Two bullet points relate to contact with the UNPROFOR people. First bullet on page 5 -- we are waiting for this to come up on our screens. You see what you said there, the second bullet point and the third bullet point on page 5. Have a look, sir, and I'll ask you my question as soon as it comes up. Thank you. Could we have that in e-court, please, P1444. Thank you. Page 11 in e-court, please. Thank you, Aleksandar. We see the English. Could we please have the Serbian, too. You see, sir, there is an entry that you made on page 5, line 4, second bullet point: "At around 1400 hours, the UN compound was seized (around 1.000 huts) in the Slapovic village sector. The compound extends from the north slopes of Zivkovo Brdo to the east of the Vagan feature - Orahovica village." That's what we explained a while ago. Thank you very much. Next bullet point, you say: "In the sector of the UN compound, the brigade commander and a group of soldiers from the brigade and a group which they had engaged as scouts captured a UN APC with five soldiers of the Dutch Battalion." Could we please go to the next page so that we can see what it says and I can ask my questions. Next page, 783, line 4, you say: "A BG, a combat group led by Captain Pajic reached Kostur and Alibegovac. Ten UN soldiers were taken prisoner at Alibegovac." Sir, bearing this in mind, your entries as well as what you told us a while ago about those men surrendering to you and you asking the corps command to take charge of them, tell us this: Were they really arrested or taken prisoner, as the wording here suggests, or did they simply surrender, as you just told us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not engaged in fighting the UN. I said taken prisoner simply because they raised their arms in surrender. It was about their own body language, not my assumption. As for the section that you just read back to me, if you look at bullet point 3 on page 5, it's quite obvious what can be concluded. In the UN compound sector, commander of the -- I said arrested, or seized, because they raised their arms in surrender because when we came down they had reached that small bridge in their APC, and when they saw us they were probably surprised. Nevertheless, I believe it's quite important in relation to previous question about the fighting, the security between Zivkovo Brdo and Vogan, a very important saddle from which one protects the access to Srebrenica, and that's where the firing came from. They fired at us. We were around the small bridge, and that included the UN men. We both came under fire, which led me to conclude that it wasn't their men firing at us. The APC was quite easy to spot. It was white. It was quite clear that that was a UN APC, therefore the firing came from the forces of the 28th Division, not the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic. This is very significant and we should know it. Even if you had arrested us, it wouldn't mean anything since their commander said that from the 9th on they were engaged against the VRS. Could the e-court please produce P590. This is a document, for the record, issued by the command of the Drina Corps which was sent from the IKM of the Drina Corps in Pribicevac on the 9th of July. It was signed by General Radislav Krstic and we are going to look at page, or, rather, paragraph 4 or bullet point 4, which says, "Conduct of UNPROFOR forces." Indeed we see it both in English and in our own Serbian language. It is now going to be blown up and you can read with me. General Krstic writes to the Main Staff: "The UNPROFOR forces at the check-points in Slapovic village and Bucje village surrendered fully to our forces with all their weapons and equipment and asked for our protection. Ten (10) UNPROFOR soldiers from the UNPROFOR check-points in Bucje village, in Bucje village, have been sent to and billeted in Milici, or accommodated in Milici, while five soldiers from the check-point in Slapovic have been accommodated in Bratunac. UNPROFOR forces from the base in Potocari village did not intervene at the check-points or attack our forces." This was signed by General Krstic. Could you please answer my following question: Bearing in mind that General Krstic informed the Main Staff in the way that we have just seen, would it be logical, based on that and based on what you have told us, for the Main Staff to conclude that they had surrendered, as General Krstic says in his report and as you testified here? Do you have any comment with this regard?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are no comments in this regard. I believe everything is clear and self-explanatory. I gave you an example of what was going on when we came in contact with the UN crew in the Slapovici sector. Obviously, there were other check-points where UN soldiers approached the VRS forces and surrendered, as it were, in order to escape areas exposed to fire. And you can see from here that they were fully protected, that they were evacuated from the theatre of war where active combat was going on. They were evacuated from that area and fully protected, as you can see in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, I would like to put a question at this point in time. We have heard different words during your conversation and the interrogation by Mr. Tolimir. We have heard the words "arrested," "taken prisoner," "captured," and "surrendered." Could you explain the different -- the meaning of the different words and descriptions of effect which has taken place? And in addition, can you explain why you use the word "captured" and "taken prisoner" in your diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to explain. Although this is my diary, this is not a combat report. I'm sure that in that combat report I would use a more adequate word. And here I only noted what was going on. I noted facts. I was not giving too much thought as to how significant this might be in a legal proceedings, so I was not really careful in choosing my words, as I would normally be. I described and I related how all that had transpired. And what can one conclude based on that? Did they surrender or not? Since we were not engaged against each other, then it wouldn't be fair to use the term that I did use, and that was that I arrested or captured somebody. But it is obvious that the people bumped into me. It was a chance meeting. I'm sure that they didn't expect that there was anybody among those houses, and I suppose that they were on their way to Zeleni Jadar because the road through Slapovic leads to their -- one of their bases in Zeleni Jadar, and all of a sudden they bumped into men from the VRS. And when they raised their arms, I just simply linked that with people being arrested. They just raised their arms, they surrendered to us. And then they lowered their arms, we collected their weapons, but we sent everything with them when the corps command representative came to take them over. And I used that term in that sense, not to describe one part of combat activities. To put it simply, I had might and they surrendered to me. They surrendered and I thought that I could use the term because that term was used after they had raised their arms, and that's a term which is used when two militaries come in contact and when they engage. And if one side, if soldiers on one side raise their arms, that means that they surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, in the order that I just quoted from, signed by Radislav Krstic, does he treat them as prisoners or does he say they surrendered? How did the command treat them and what kind of a report was sent to the Main Staff in respect of those men?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, if I have the right to do so, to suggest that that was not an order, it was an interim combat report. And if that's the document that we are talking about, the one that is on the screen now, the corps command treats UNPROFOR troops as men who had surrendered to our forces, and who had sought our protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for everything. Thank you for correcting me. This is not an order. It is indeed a combat report. Could you please tell us, what happened to those men next? Where were they accommodated? Were they accommodated in a prison? Were they kept in custody? Were they accommodated somewhere else? Were they treated as prisoners of war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not in a prison, they were not kept in any kind of custody, they were not remanded in custody. As far as I heard, I believe that they linked up with their forces and they continued carrying out their tasks, given to them by the battalion commander but they did not remain in the area. They were moved from the area and they continued working as soldiers until the moment they left the sector altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic. Do you perhaps know that they were accommodated in the Bratunac Hotel and that an UNPROFOR representative inspected their accommodation when he came to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know where they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could this document -- I apologise, I've just received information that it has been admitted into evidence. Thank you. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, in view of the situation that you described in your diary surrounding Zeleni Jadar, for the transcript, we have to say whether you arrested any UN troops in that settlement. You call it a UN settlement. Was that indeed a UN settlement or was it something that was constructed by the Swedish government for refugees and was it under protection of the UN?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I called it that because I believe that it was built with donation of the Red Cross, so instead of going at great length describing what it was, I just called it a UN compound or settlement. But it was not where UN forces were billeted; it was a refugee settlement of prefabricated houses. I believe that the donation had come from Norway. It was a very huge plain field with houses, so as I was looking at it from the hill top I don't think that there were more than 500 houses. Here in my diary I mention the figure of 1.000, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. If it assists the Trial Chamber, I think the Prosecution - I don't think there will be any dispute from the Defence - can represent to the Court that the location we are talking about, this settlement, is known as "the Swedish shelter project." I think the Trial Chamber has heard reference to this location from a number of witnesses, I don't think there is any dispute, but just to perhaps help orient everyone and for the record in the future, I think that's what we are talking about and perhaps we can just come to an agreement so we know exactly what this location is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this suggestion. Do you agree with that, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I agree. I don't object. Can we see a photo of that project, if it will only take a minute and not longer? We simply don't have time to watch a lengthy video clip. I have one minute, so could Mr. Thayer provide a reference number to the e-court? But only one minute. Not longer. There is simply not enough time to watch a long video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not the request of the Prosecution, as I understood Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. President, I'm not aware of any video footage of the Swedish shelter project. Perhaps the Defence is aware, but I'm not aware of any video of that location. Certainly not from this -- from July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, have you ever heard this term, "Swedish shelter project"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. To be honest, I've never heard of a Swedish shelter project, but I believe that I understand Mr. Thayer's intention. If he refers to a shelter as a refugee settlement where people were sheltered in prefabricated houses, then yes, I agree that this term can be used. It was a Swedish project for refugees houses. Obviously at that time I didn't know that. I thought that that was a UN settlement, not necessarily a Swedish settlement. But I believe that the prefabricated houses had come from Swedish -- Sweden, hence the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope this clarified the situation. I was a little afraid that the assistance of Mr. Thayer would confuse everybody, but I think we can leave it like it is and Mr. Tolimir should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, you have just told us that fire was opened by Muslim units from Srebrenica on your troops and on UNPROFOR troops, and that happened in Slapovici village. And you also spoke about human shield, what the meaning of that was. And you said that UNPROFOR used Muslims as human shields. What can you tell us about that? Were there indeed such situations and was their fire a response to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday I spoke about that term when I said that people were used as shield to cover activities of the enemy side. I believe that they continued to pursue that practice and those activities, and that could be observed in Srebrenica and later on in Zepa, from a check-point that was in the Borak sector. Other forces were there, but also UNPROFOR forces were there, but I never claimed that UNPROFOR opened fire on my unit. However, the two check-points were so close to each other that they made use of the situation and opened fire from a close vicinity on our forces just to create an impression that we came under the fire of the international community. That's how they tried and managed to disguise their own activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic. I'll repeat: You said a human shield. That's your reference. Your words, not mine. At page 1188 of the transcript from the Popovic trial, the question was, why were they scared and why did they surrender to you? The UNPROFOR men. Your answer, I'm quoting your answer: "I think they said they were scared of the men of the 28th Division who had been using them as a human shield. It was for that reason that they moved over to the VRS." That was what my question was about when I asked you whether you remember being told that. You said so yesterday and I just wanted you to state that for the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that can be concluded from what I said a minute ago, just worded differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke a minute ago about the fact that you never fired at UNPROFOR. Do you know whether the corps command at the Main Staff ever issued an order to any of the subordinate units to attack UNPROFOR for as long as you were engaged in combat and in close contact there, throughout the situations on the 9th and 10th, which is what you're talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I heard of. I don't know whether such orders were given to anyone else, but if I was given no such orders, it's quite likely that no one else was either. No such orders were issued at any of the meetings that I attended. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Speaking of UNPROFOR and combat operations, in the Popovic trial you spoke about Muslim acts of provocation vis-a-vis UNPROFOR. It was about air-strikes against VRS positions, at page 11D00, line 25, and then 11D00, line 5, you said, and I quote you, since neither of us speak English: "At the time, based on intelligence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? It is absolutely unclear which part of the Popovic transcript you are referring to. Please say the number, the page number again, and I would like to mention that the Popovic transcript is P1197. Please repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive any interpretation at the moment. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, Popovic transcript 11900 is the page number, line 25, and then 11901, line 5, where the witness said as follows. Here, we can see that in English on our screens and I'll read to the witness what he said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "At the time, based on the intelligence that arrived from superior commands, and based on the intelligence that we received from our men on the ground, there was some mention of it. Later on, as I studied some documents, I came to know, based on General Smith's statement, that he, in fact, proposed it to the UN units themselves, or rather, the UN representatives, who were to convey this to the Security Council." As far as I understand, all this is about is how to provoke a decision on the use of NATO forces. Is my understanding correct, sir? And can you please explain for the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did mention that in the Popovic trial. Also about sorties made by the helicopters flying over VRS positions. There were two statements that were made, one in the capacity of an expert, the other in the capacity of a witness. General Smith, at least in the Serbian translation, claims that he initiated for the sorties to be approved in order to provoke VRS action, fire on those helicopters carrying humanitarian aid, which would have effectively given a green light for the NATO air force to be used to attack VRS positions. And that was as much as I could glean from the statements that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are embarking on a group of questions to do with the use of NATO air force. This is something that you described at page 9, the ERN number is 0648-6791. This is Exhibit 1444. Could we please have that in e-court and shown to the witness. Thank you. Page 9 in the Serbian. The last three ERN digits, 791.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen. Please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me just read what he wrote there, the first line on this page, and I'll base my question on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Line 1 on this page, sir, you wrote: "At around 1330 hours --" and that is line 4 in the English -- "General Mladic gave notice to us to get ready and use camouflage (troops and combat equipment, as well as materiel and technical supplies) because of the threat of NATO air-strikes." Next bullet point same page: "At around 1400 hours --" half an hour after General Mladic's warning --" aircraft flew over three times, attacking the road on which my command group, the hardware we used, were on." Thank you. Based on this entry in your diary, sir, my question would be: First of all, after General Mladic's order, did you use all the camouflage methods, such as burning stacks of hay in order to create sources of heat to fool the radars and all other methods of camouflage warfare? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units were in a number of different positions. I'm talking specifically about my own unit. The position of my command group and me was along an asphalt road between Bojna and Srebrenica. There were some trees, a forest there, and people tried to disguise or camouflage their vehicles, their combat and command vehicles, or supply vehicles even. The men who were on that road, and that included me and my group, took shelter under a huge tree that was next to that road. This was all on a slope. The units on the front line, the units engaged in the fighting further off from the road, we had conveyed that signal about the air-strikes and they did what they could, depending on their positions. Nevertheless, all of the air-strikes targeted that road with so many vehicles and commands along it. Somebody made an accurate assessment that that road was a primary target because so many things were there. The command groups would have found it impossible to be set up or settle in any other area but along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, before the air-strikes, this particular attack that occurred at 1400 hours that you describe, did you have any contacts with any APCs or soldiers belonging to UNPROFOR who were in the Srebrenica protected enclave?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've answered that question. That was the previous day, the 9th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You're quite right. My question, what about the 11th? On that day did you have any contact with the UN in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing all of this in mind, then what you said about your contacts with the UN, the NATO air-strikes, do you know about anything indicating that the NATO air-strikes were provoked, that they attacked you because of something else that was going on on the ground that provoked them to take steps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything specific that would lead me to make that conclusion. The only thing is the direction had been changed so the NATO forces, and probably also the monitoring equipment used to monitor the movement of units throughout that area, perhaps that was in contact with General Mladic at about 1330, and maybe that blocked -- that was blocked by the NATO air-strikes, if you head down that road in that direction at the time, but not that anyone told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you very much. And do you perhaps know that NATO later justified their use of air-strikes because allegedly five UN soldiers were taken prisoner in that village? Did you ever learn that that was what triggered the NATO attack, as witnesses in this trial have testified? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask for a specific reference. If it's being put to this witness that the alleged justification for NATO air-strikes was this particular taking prisoner of five UN soldiers as being the reason for the NATO air-strikes, I think it's incumbent upon the accused to provide exactly what he's talking about. I think the Trial Chamber is familiar with the testimony on this general topic, and I'm curious as to what the general is referring to here as being the basis for this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you give a reference? Mr. Tolimir, are you able to give a reference for this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- for the way you put this question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Mr. Thayer. Until a reference is found, I can assume that Mr. Egbers said it in his evidence. He dispatched a reconnaissance patrol to look for our forces. They called back to say that they had been captured in such and such a village, where the Swedish settlement was. My legal assistant will locate the reference during my examination, and will be providing the details soon enough. Nevertheless, he said that UNPROFOR men had been captured at Slapovici. Until the exact reference is found, we can go on and talk about some other topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... your question without this reference, and the question was did you ever learn that that was what triggered the NATO attack? Would you please give us your opinion, what was the trigger for the NATO attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard anyone say -- I personally never heard anyone say that the capture of the five DutchBat soldiers in the Slapovici sector was what triggered this operation on the 11th of July. There could have been threats being made at the time all this was going on, on the 9th, but now we are looking at the 11th, and I see no link between the 9th, the capture of those men, and the air-strikes. I'm unable to establish a link between the two. So I don't think that's what triggered it. I gave you my own reflections a while ago. My personal conclusion, based on General Mladic's warning, a circular communication to each of the commanders, he personally addressed us, telling us to be ready for these strikes and to start camouflaging. It is quite obvious that he had been in touch with someone or other. My conclusion is the threat stemmed most probably, and I can't be certain, from the change of direction and the process of getting closer to Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, could you please tell me whether NATO forces and UNPROFOR forces had a task to protect Srebrenica if resistance was put up from there and if it refused to be disarmed, or was NATO used to stop the activities of the VRS? In other words, what was the reason to use NATO?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have a task to protect Srebrenica in the sense of any prevention. Their main task was to separate the two forces, and their presence was meant to prevent both sides from attacking. At the moment when this task was carried out on the 11th, their role was still to protect both sides. I suppose that that's the general role of the United Nations, to take measures to prevent unnecessary losses. And I believe that the unnecessary losses could have been caused by NATO air-strikes, if they were the ones that called for NATO air-strikes. My units did not open fire on the town, on the areas where people had already started gathering. Nobody fired a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're saying that you didn't open fire either on Muslims or the UNPROFOR but still you came under a NATO attack. You were targeted by NATO. My question is this: Based on what you've told us about what you know why you became targeted, do you know that on the 11th, in the evening, the UNPROFOR commander held a meeting with Muslim armed forces and that he informed them that on the following morning there would be NATO air-strikes on that axis, that he asked them to withdraw from that axis, and his explanation was that there would be NATO air-strikes and he warned them to withdraw unless they wanted to become targets of those NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a correction. I think General Tolimir misspoke. We are talking about, I think he's referring to the evening of the 10th, not the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir? Are you referring to the evening of 10th or the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I mentioned the night between the 10th and the 11th. The witness has testified here about the meeting between Colonel Karremans and Muslim military leaders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not necessary to go further. It was just a correction of page 22, line 11. You were recorded having said the 11th in the evening, but, in fact, you mean the night between the 10th and the 11th. That's enough. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I misspoke. I used the word 11 first and then I corrected myself and I used the words 10 and 11, so I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, do you know that Karremans met with Muslim military leaders and civilians and that he told them that NATO strikes would occur on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was not aware of that. Nobody ever informed me about that. Nobody was duty-bound to inform me, as a matter of fact, in view of my role. However, later on, I read in some statements and documents, in some publications, and a book which was published by one of the DutchBat officers, that a meeting did take place, however, I did not have any contemporaneous knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind all those things that you've read and what I have just told you and the fact that at that meeting Karremans did announce that everything around one kilometre area around Srebrenica would be destroyed, including all the military positions and check-points, would you be able to conclude, based on that, why you and your unit was targeted without ever having opened fire either on UNPROFOR or the civilian population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D2D9 [as interpreted], and in the meantime, perhaps Mr. Thayer can say what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just note that General Tolimir asked the witness a question that the witness simply agreed with, yes, but didn't actually answer the question. And I think to make the record clear, rather than just simply agreeing with General Tolimir's question, there is actually a question there that needs to be answered. I think if you just read the question, you'll see what my intervention is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, did you understand what Mr. Thayer said? And I would like to repeat: Would you be able to conclude, based on that, why you and your unit was targeted without ever having opened fire either on UNPROFOR or the civilian population? That was the question of Mr. Tolimir. Why, is the question. And to say yes is not an answer to the question why. Have you any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will excuse me, I'm completely confused now. What question am I now supposed to answer? What did I not answer? Perhaps General Tolimir or perhaps you, Mr. President, could define the question completely. I certainly don't want to be perceived as somebody who just says yes, who just agrees with what they hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question of Mr. Tolimir was why -- would you be able to conclude, based on that, what Mr. Tolimir put to you, why you and your unit was targeted without ever having opened fire either on UNPROFOR or the civilian population? Why were you targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I have to say that it was not just me but all the command groups that were on that road as well as combat vehicles and units along the road. Not only my unit but also my -- the units of my right flank neighbour. If it is true that the meeting took place on the 10th of July and that UNPROFOR command indeed suggested that the forces should withdraw as far away as possible from the area which would be targeted by the air -- NATO air-strikes the following morning, I'm sure that all of the previous activities of the VRS and the change of our axis of attack had been used as a pretext for air-strikes, and I suppose that the Muslim forces were advised to withdraw in order to avoid becoming victims. If indeed the Muslim side was warned, it is obvious that nothing but a pretext was sought to enter the city and to target the city, and if all that happened on the 10th of July in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is your answer. And now Mr. Tolimir should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, when we are talking about NATO and UNPROFOR, do they have the right to change the balance of powers? You said that the main reason was to prevent you from entering Srebrenica and changing your course of action. Do they have the right to engage in activities that will change the balance of powers on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that they have the right. I don't think that they should have -- should be -- behave the way they did, if there are indeed indicia that they behaved for a reason in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have just told us that if it is true that the NATO strikes were announced and that's why they behaved the way they did, could you please look at the document which is now in front of you, which speaks precisely about that. That is a transcript from the Srebrenica's Death Fields documentary, produced by radio television of Serbia, and broadcast on 9 July 2010. And the guests were those that speak on this page. Thank you, Aleksandar. Their statements were broadcast during that show. Here you can see Hakija Meholjic, a member of the Srebrenica War Presidency, who in the period between 1993 and 1995, and he says: "In the meantime, Karremans arrived --" and I'm quoting him and I'm repeating for the benefit of the record. Hakija Meholjic says, and I quote: In the meantime, Karremans arrived, requesting a meeting, and I told him five more minutes, we can agree first because we have no reason to trust you anymore. We arranged everything, then we received him --" and I mean Karremans --" for a talk and he said that NATO had informed him that that zone had been set around a Srebrenica for tomorrow at half past five. Everything that moved on two, four or 100 feet, or on a hundred wheels or on one wheel or two wheels, would be destroyed. And get -- then he repeats, it would be destroyed. And then the second participant in the meeting, who was the interpreter at that meeting, Hasan Nuhanovic, and I quote Hasan Nuhanovic: "The Serbian side was given an ultimatum to withdraw by 0600 hours to their starting position, in other words, Zeleni Jadar, to go back six kilometres or they would be bombarded at 0600 hours. And they said that the number of aircraft that would come for the air-strike, they told me, would be between 40 and 70. That's what they said." Mr. Hasan Nuhanovic was Mr. Karremans' interpreter at the meeting. Bearing all of this in mind, bearing in mind what I have just read out to you, and I'm not suggesting an answer to you -- in other words, my question should have followed after this. Let me ask you again: Do NATO forces have the right to change the balance of powers, the military powers of the opposing side by any of their actions? That was the goal of my question and that was the reason why I quoted what I did. But you have already answered that question and you told us that they don't have the right to do that. If you want to do so, you can repeat that question or say something else in response to my question, which is the same as the one before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that was indeed a very long question and I'm quite confused now. You should try to put a very clear question to a witness. I didn't understand that. And in fact, I don't know which document we have on the screen now because that was not recorded properly on page 24, line 1. Could you, for the sake of the record, please repeat the number. And it's better to put a question to a witness instead of giving a long explanation and then say you have answered this question already. Please, again, the number of this document and then your question to the witness in a very short way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is 1D238, for the record. And this was a programme publicly broadcast on the 9th of July 2010, on Radio Television of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was only asking you for the number because that was not recorded. Thank you, and now put your question to the witness in a way which is not confusing the witness and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, in view of the fact that Mr. Karremans, through his interpreter, at the meeting with the Muslim military leadership said that NATO had informed him about the air-strike that would happen the following day and that that indeed happened on the following day, on the 11th, could you have been targeted, bearing in mind the words of the witnesses who had attended that meeting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If these statements are correct, and if it is true that that was discussed, and if reference was made to an area of six kilometres around Srebrenica, I'm sure that my unit and the other units of the VRS would have been exposed to the air-strikes. And in the document currently on e-court I can only say or, rather, I can add to that that Meholjic has been saying these things for years during election campaigns in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In those campaigns, he has publicly spoken about what was going on in Srebrenica during the war, and the policy of the government in Sarajevo towards Srebrenica, according to him, when he was running for a member of the Presidency of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he stated that Alija Izetbegovic wanted to sacrifice several thousand people in order to provoke NATO air-strikes against the Serbs. And similar things happened in other republics while Yugoslavia was breaking up, and this is an ongoing theory and these statements have already been heard many times from Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you said that this is 1D238, but I was told by the Registry it is 1D239, for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for drawing my attention to that. I misstated the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, did NATO act without a decision by the Security Council when they used the air force in the Srebrenica enclave? Do we have anything by the Security Council on the air-strikes against the VRS in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for certain whether there is anything or not. Nevertheless, because of their actions, throughout the break-up of Yugoslavia, leading up to the last air-strikes carried out during the operation known as the Merciful Angel aimed at Serbia, I don't think the Security Council actually okayed any of those air-strikes or operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was NATO signatory to the demilitarisation agreement, and was it entitled to shift the balance of powers pursuant to that agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not privy to the detail of that agreement and therefore not willing to commit on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk about Zepa. You were no longer involved in combat activities later on, after Srebrenica was taken. You were sent to Zepa. May I remind you of page 11903, lines 17 through 22, the transcript from the Popovic trial, you talked about the assessment of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, P1197.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote your words, 11903. P1197 is the document number. "There was an assessment --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the number. The interpreter didn't understand the number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The assessment said between 500 and 700 men arrived from the Srebrenica enclave after our forces had entered Srebrenica. There were some elements of their forces that refused to be disarmed. And they were on their way from Srebrenica to Zepa. Therefore, I assume there were between 2.000 and 2.500 members of the BH Army there." My question, based on what I've just read to you, can you tell us whether you have anything else to base your assessment on? And did this assessment prove to be correct eventually? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've nothing to add to the statement I made. I think the accuracy of this assessment was proved on the ground, and also everything that happened in the Zvornik Brigade defence area proved it. I stand by my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see later that you also speak about operations conducted by APCs. What about the ratios that you address here in terms of weapons and combat capacity? Would that not increase if one obtained the information indicating that the Muslim forces in Zepa were using the combat equipment and technology made available to them by UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If UNPROFOR combat technology was used, it certainly increased their fire power, the firepower of the Muslim forces. I don't think I ever stated that this was confirmed. The assumption certainly was that they were using the combat technology of the Ukrainian Battalion from UNPROFOR, or that at least they were operating under their protection, as I said earlier today. During your first questions, I talked about the fact that they were operating under UN protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we please now have D105. D105. Thank you. Could we please have that on our screens. Before that comes up, let me say that this is a BH army document. It's 285th Light Mountain Brigade from Zepa. The document was signed by Avdo Palic. Could we please look at line 11, which says: "We are disarming UNPROFOR in accordance with the directive we received earlier on. This was produced on the 16th of July 1995 and was signed by the commander of the forces in Zepa, Colonel Avdo Palic." What does this indicate? Does it not indicate the same thing that you were saying, sir, that APCs in the possession of UNPROFOR in Zepa were firing at you? Thank you very much. I'll provide a quote later on, but you did say that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that. And this confirms my earlier statement and my assumptions regarding the fact that observations were made about those APCs firing machine-guns and other guns, whatever types of weapons were mounted on the APCs at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: 11868 is the page, lines 15 through 18, of the transcript in the Popovic trial. You said as follows: "I was not informed about the progress of the negotiations on the 19th. We were told that we were to stop all activities because a cease-fire had been signed, or maybe it wasn't signed yet but had been agreed." Earlier on, you said they were using UNPROFOR weapons and equipment to attack your unit. I just wanted to remind you of the date. What can you tell us about that event when they used anti-aircraft weapons to fire at your units, your men? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing special to say about that. You try to put up with it but you try to take shelter, you try to inform your superior commander what's going on. Obviously, I was criticised for that. It was very difficult. I failed in completing that mission. I couldn't take that elevation, I couldn't take the trig point that we wanted to take, and there was this white APC -- the firing did not occur immediately after the unit had started engaging the enemy, and several days later I suppose the report went there about the disarming of these forces. Here UNPROFOR forces, I think that was several days later on, and then taking over all this combat equipment, and it wasn't before they actually took that APC that fire was opened. And when I link it all up in this context, one thing leads to the other, and then there was one of the previous documents, the reports of Avdo Palic. And now I can put two and two together and tell you what the picture adds up to. It was exactly like this, so this has now proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have the first break now, but before we break, I would like to ask you, are you tendering the document you have used, 1D239? We have seen one page of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes indeed. Thank you for reminding me. We are tendering that document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have seen only one page. How many pages does this transcript of a documentary encompass?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sure you will remember this has been shown twice in court. It's a very short video clip. It's an excerpt from a documentary for Republic of Serbia TV. What we saw here on our screens is the document. Just a single page, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D00137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, the Chamber admits the document 65 ter 00108, which was previously assigned P1225 and marked for identification, and I will leave it in the hands of the Registry to assign a P or a D number. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for consistency of the records, I believe we should maintain the P number, which is P1225, but it will technically be a document that is admitted via the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have the first break now. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before we broke, the witness wanted to have back D1005. If he could see that in e-court, the witness would like to have another look. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This must be a mistake again. I think it should be D105.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is indeed right. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see the document, Witness, so you can tell us whatever you wanted to say about this document.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just trying to establish a link between my previous assertion and this document. If all of this is true, then the fire that came from a UN vehicle really did occur. We see that Avdo Palic informs someone that they were disarming UNPROFOR in accordance with the directives that they had received. It is quite obvious that they didn't do that for the first couple of days, they didn't carry out their task in that area, and then an APC was used for operations holding a crew of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The date here is the 16th. We can use that as a reference point. My next question: It's about the cease-fire that you mentioned. The document number P1444, ERN number 821, page 50 in e-court. You talked about the cease-fire. Can you please have a look and then I'll ask you my question. Thank you. We don't see you reporting here that there was a cease-fire. Can you please tell us what you had in mind when you said you were asked on the 19th, on the 18th and the 19th, your entries to the logbook, the cease-fire? Can you tell us, was that the first cease-fire? And how exactly were you requested to make that order? I'll try to find the exact page of your diary in e-court. I'm facing some difficulties finding my way around.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My original reflects the 19th of July. The -- if you flip page 9 on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the ERN number on my original copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, can you be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps if we were able to hand up the ERN'd version. I'm happy to make the transition but for etiquette purposes we needs the assistance of the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It was handed over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 9, 0648-6828. That's the ERN number for you. The other side, 6829, the other side of that page. No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph reads the cease-fire was signed that evening, the Zepa people surrendered. At about 1900 hours a cease-fire was ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is, I find it very difficult to find my way around your entries. What is the date for this entry and what date is the entry in relation to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we go back one page to 6828, we'll see where Colonel Trivic began with his answer, which he said was his handwritten page 9, and there is that entry for 19 July, Wednesday. And since we are at the Zepa section, we are working our way backwards through the notebook. If we go back one more page to the flip side of this page, which is 6827, at the top of the page, we'll see the continuation of his entry from the 19th of July, at the top of this page, which is 6827. "In the evening, a truce was signed." That was the portion he was just reading, and that continues from 6828. That's just the flip side of 6828 because we are, again, working our way backwards through the document. And I presume the witness can confirm, but I think that's what he was more or less saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, could you confirm that this was a correct introduction into your diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is correct. The general asked me a question about how I made these entries. On the first day, I believe, Mr. Thayer and I explained how I drew up a summary of the 25th of July. I summed up everything, I updated the strength of our unit, the number of injured, and the progress of combat operations up until the 24th, and then on the 25th I made these entries in relation to the several days just before. So it wasn't in reference to that day, this entry. It was just by way of a summary. If you look at list number 7, that is exactly what it shows. ERN 832. It goes from 832 backwards to the 26th. And it is from there on that the regular records resume. At 1900 hours on the 26th, I again updated everything in relation to that date. That is in answer to the general's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Trivic. You have now clarified this for us and the information is in relation to the 19th, as Mr. Thayer just said. There is something that I'd like to read to you, what Alija Izetbegovic told them on the 19th, the evening of the 19th, after the cease-fire that was signed. Could we please have D54, D54 in e-court, please. Thank you. Mehmed Efendija Hajric, Zepa president, encrypted conversation with Alija Izetbegovic. He says: "Dear Mr. President. Here are my answers to your questions of last night." Now let's skip to paragraph 3. We see this is Efendija Hajric from Zepa. He's answering Alija Izetbegovic and addressing him as Dear Mr. President. Paragraph 3 reads: "My plan. Move out as many of my civilians as possible and all of them, if possible. The troops stay on and continue to resist. We will do everything we can to help you by supplying MTS. Volunteers and offensive action in your direction, I believe this is starting today. If we do not succeed in this, you try to push your way through along those roads, you know which, but now without the burden of women and children who would in the meantime have been pulled out already. In addition to this plan, there is another plan on the joint withdrawal across the mountains prepared by Dr. Heljic and his team. I think that plan is much more difficult. Delic thinks it's unrealistic. I'm sending you a shortened version and you will get the idea." If we look at the signature, we see My Salaams to Avdo and all the others. So Alija Izetbegovic is sending this to the president of Zepa, war president of Zepa, Mehmed Efendija Hajric on the 19th of July. This person was involved, as we are about to see later on, in the disarming process. My question: If you read paragraph 3 where they talk about the evacuation of the Muslim army, based on the 19th, when we signed the cease-fire, can one not see that the Muslim representatives have no commitment to actually pull their army out along with the civilians without passing through the woods and fighting their way out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This obviously arises from the text. They were adamant not to surrender their weapons. And they opted for other ways to retreat from Srebrenica under arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that several cease-fire agreements were signed later on, which you recorded in your diary on the 24th, for example, and so on and so forth, please tell us this: Did the Muslim side negotiate only to buy time for the retreat of the army, as described in this document, and all they wanted to do was to send their women and children away?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the objective, in my view, and you can see it in paragraph 3. It says here that everything will be done by supplying MTS, volunteers and offensive action in their direction so as to allow them to continue fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As the commander of the unit, or one of the units that was moving towards Zepa, marching towards Zepa, did you feel on the ground that the Muslims behaved in keeping with the instructions that they had received from their president, irrespective of the fact that they had signed the cease-fire agreement and that their wives and children had been released by us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was obvious. The fighting continued, and in keeping with that, when the cease-fire had been agreed at the corps level, I received the task to continue putting up resistance and fight those that were still fighting us despite the fact that we had signed the cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your notebook, you recorded, on the 24th, that women and children were being evacuated. Maybe you can find it. I've lost my bearings in your diary. Can you find that entry and can you tell us whether, after the 24th of July, the Muslim forces continued fighting the VRS despite the fact that their women and children were being evacuated across the VRS territory into the territory under the control of the Federation army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so. On the 24th of July, we experienced a crucial event for my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to interrupt you. What side of your diary are you reading from? And what is your -- the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6823 is the ERN -- are the four digits, the last four digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mean the last three digits?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 823, the last three digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told we have again a problem with e-court. The document can't be loaded up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is page 52 in e-court. Maybe you can locate that page under that number. Page 52 in e-court, and the document number is P1444. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The technical problem is resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you go to the following page of the document, where there is a reference to that cease-fire agreement. Thank you, Mr. Trivic. Could you please answer my question? We don't want to waste any more time in locating all the different pages and finding our bearings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All we need to do, Mr. President, is just go back one page, to 6822, and there will be an entry, I think, for the 25th of July. I believe that's the entry to which General Tolimir is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 25th I recorded that there was no combat, the cease-fire order was being honoured, we are monitoring the evacuation of the enemy civilians and the wounded. Organisational replenishment with MTS and ammunition, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what you just said and based on my previous question, did Muslims continue fighting even after the 25th, after the evacuation -- their Muslim -- their women and children had been evacuated across the VRS territory to the territory under the control of the Federation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this indicate that they behaved in keeping with the instructions that they had received from the government in Sarajevo and that was to try to organise the retreat of their troops and not of their surrender?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One might be inclined to conclude that in addition to the evacuation of the civilians and the wounded, that they continued to adhere to their plan, and that plan was to break through fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, I am slightly confused in the moment. The entry we have on the screen now, 6822 is the ERN number, you wrote down, "There were no combat operations," and then the next line, "The order to cease-fire and fortify line reacheds (sic) is being observed." Was there fire or was there not fire? I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Let me find that in the original. This is page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 12. Your entry about the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've missed that. Page 12, 25th of July, when I said a while ago that they continued fighting while pulling out members of the brigade under arms from the area, you can see from the diary that there were days without any action or operations, and as soon as one batch of civilians and wounded was pulled out, once it was left, the action and the operations continued. Hence, the confusion. On the 24th, there were actions after the cease-fire was signed and observed, and we protect the lines reached. When I said we protect the lines reached, that means we were digging shelters, finding places where we would wait for the night. This is a military term which implies manning positions to avoid any unpleasant surprises and losses. The third bullet point for the 25th is: Work on evacuating enemy civilians and wounded, organisational replenishment with MTS, and so on and so forth. I believe that you can now understand. And on the 26th of July, the situation was somewhat different. On the 26th of July, with your leave, this is on the next page, or, rather, on the flip page -- flip side of page 12, the ERN number is 821, the whole day, until the evening, there were no operations. And then on the 26th, at 1900 hours, I recorded the following: The evacuation is -- of civilians from Zepa is proceeding according to plan. So far, around two-thirds of inhabitants have been evacuated, the rest are boarding now. Some other problems have appeared. Fear of what the civilians might do, of their actions. This is just a little note to record the things that were happening. Order to search the area that is now under the control of my unit. My unit had taken that territory and established its control in the area. We ordered them -- the troops to search the area, to scour the ground to prevent any unpleasant surprises from the remaining elements of the Zepa Brigade. And that is why there were days without any action or fire, but as soon as the activities surrounding the evacuation was finished, the actions started and fire was opened, and that's how I -- I ended up wounded on the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic, you've answered made next question. Or rather, my next question is this: Despite the numerous violations of cease-fire, after the civilians left from Zepa, did Muslims continue to organise active operations, inflicting damages on the VRS? And you've just told us that you were wounded in that period. Do you want to answer that again? Do you have anything to add to what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your diary, on ERN number 0648-61 [as interpreted] of the same document that we have on the screen, the document number is 819, can this please be shown in e-court? And in e-court this is 45, I believe, but I'm not sure. I believe that that's the case. I really can't find my bearings again. I can't find the thing again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The ERN number is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 819. ERN number is 0648-6819, page 48 in electronic court. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness (sic) please slow down for the benefit of everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You noted next to the exclamation mark -- we could say that this is the third paragraph. This is what you noted: "I strictly prohibit torching of houses!" Who is it who prohibits that? Whose order was that that you recorded in the diary? Was that your order or the order of your commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, this is the continuation of the contents that begins on the 26th of July on page 821 in e-court. That's at 1900 hours. Then it continues on 820, and we come to 819. I recorded, and highlighted this: "I strictly prohibit torching of houses." This was a task issued by the corps commander. Obviously my arrival at the unit implies the conveyance of that order to my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we now look at something in e-court, if we look at the document at 0648-6816, which is number 15 in your diary, we will see that this is an entry which was made on the 25th, or, rather, the 26th and it's page 45, and we'll see where you say in the second paragraph, and I'm going to read it, and I quote your words: "From the IKM I was asked --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. The interpreters really have to work very hard to follow your reading and your explanations. And the same applies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading from this page that we can see on the screen, paragraph 2, from the IKM of the Drina Corps, I was asked to take measures to prevent torching of houses and that I was responsible for any such actions. The following bullet point: I visited the unit and I established the following: That it was done by a company of the Bratunac Brigade which had come as reinforcements the night before. Thank you, end of quote and my question is this: Did the corps command take any measures against those who disobeyed the order not torch houses? Was it done by the corps command? Can we see that from your notes, from the document in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was done. The measures undertaken by the corps command and which I recorded and highlighted with a -- with the exclamation mark, that means that on the 25th, in the evening, there was a problem of houses being torched during the night. You can see that I tried to investigate who had done that, and then on the 26th, the commander again highlighted all that and that's why I put the exclamation mark next to my entry. He asked me to discuss that with my officers and to report back to the corps command on what had happened, and you can see from the contents that it was the Bratunac Brigade, or one -- some of the elements of the Bratunac Brigade that came on my strength when I had asked for reinforcement, after we had crossed the bridgehead and I wanted to reinforce the security of the area that I had taken. Measures were indeed taken against the men who were behaving in an irresponsible way and destroyed property without any need whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Trivic. A while ago you said you were wounded. Can you tell us when and where? And when, what day? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 29th of July, that afternoon, at the Zepske Kolibe plateau. There was firing there. There was an elevation there called Zlovrh with a communications hut. Just before reaching that feature, at a distance of about 200 or 300 metres, fire was opened on a group that I was with. I received a gunshot wound. It came from a rifle. There was group of us, between 10 and 15 officers. Another soldier was killed, one received a wound to the arm, and I too was shot. That was on the 29th. Combat operations had been announced.
